\chapter{Twenty, a Hundred, and the Nine Words That Are Not Here}
\label{ch:ur-round-amounts}
\hlchaptermodality{30}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count aloud, say twenty and a hundred, and say why Urdu's eleven to nineteen are nine separate words rather than a rule.}

The two round amounts a price actually names, the pair a noisy counter confuses, and an explicit account of what the teens cost and why they wait.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bīs]{\ur{بیس} — twenty, and the nine words that are not in this chapter}

\label{lesson:UR-C30-bees}



\begin{quote}
Count one to ten, then say ten on its own.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{بیس}} — \emph{bīs} — \textbf{twenty}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{بیس}} goes back through Sanskrit \emph{vimshati} to the Indo-European word for twenty, the same word behind Latin \textbf{vīgintī} and, through it, English \textbf{vigesimal}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what is NOT here, and why}]
Eleven to nineteen are missing from this book on purpose, and the reason is a fact about Urdu rather than a shortage of pages.

Some languages build their teens. Persian, next door, puts a unit in front of its word for ten and stops: \emph{yâz}-dah, \emph{si}-dah, \emph{chahâr}-dah — nine numbers from one rule.

\textbf{Urdu does not.} \emph{gyārah}, \emph{bārah}, \emph{terah}, \emph{chaudah}, \emph{pandrah}, \emph{solah}, \emph{satrah}, \emph{aṭhārah}, \emph{unnīs} — the ten is worn down differently in almost every one, and the unit with it. They are nine words, not one pattern, and the same is true of every number up to ninety-nine.

So they belong to a tranche of their own rather than to this one, and saying so is more useful than pretending a rule exists. What this book gives you instead is the frame the teens will hang on: \textbf{ek} to \textbf{das} below, \textbf{bīs} above.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{bīs} — twenty
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{bīs} $\leftarrow$ Sanskrit \emph{vimshati} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{wikmtih} $\to$ Latin \textbf{vīgintī}
  \item \emph{Say why:} Urdu's teens are nine words, not one rule
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sau]{\ur{سو} — a hundred}

\label{lesson:UR-C30-sau}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{bīs}, then \textbf{nau}, then the other word \textbf{\ur{نو}} can spell.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{سو}} — \emph{sau} — \textbf{a hundred}
\end{quote}

Two letters: the \textbf{\ur{س}} that opens seven and the \textbf{\ur{و}} that closes nine. The largest number in this book is the shortest word in it.

Say \textbf{\ur{نو}} and \textbf{\ur{سو}} one after the other. One consonant apart, and a hundred apart in value — which is exactly where a price is misheard at a busy counter, so drill them as a pair.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{سو}} continues Sanskrit \emph{śata}, from Indo-European *\emph{kmtom}, \textquotedblleft{}hundred.\textquotedblright{} Latin \textbf{centum}, Greek \textbf{hekatón} and English \textbf{hundred} are the same word. Anybody who has read a \textbf{per cent} has met its cousin.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{sau} — a hundred
  \item \emph{Pair:} \textbf{nau} and \textbf{sau} — one consonant, a hundredfold
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{das, bīs, sau} — the three round amounts
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — counting aloud, and the three round amounts}

\label{lesson:UR-C30-practice}



\begin{quote}
Count one to ten, then say why eleven to nineteen are not in this book yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Four skills, scored separately.

\begin{enumerate}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Count aloud} one to ten without a model, then say \textbf{bīs} and \textbf{sau}.
  \item \textbf{Listening.} Hear twelve amounts named singly and out of order and write each down in figures of your own language.
  \item \textbf{Reading.} Read the twelve printed shuffled and say each.
  \item \textbf{Writing.} Write all twelve from dictation, shuffled.
\end{enumerate}

Then say the three amounts a shop is likeliest to name — \textbf{das}, \textbf{bīs}, \textbf{sau} — and the pair a noisy counter confuses: \textbf{nau} and \textbf{sau}.

An A1 examiner asks a candidate their age, the price of something and a telephone number. Before this slice none of the three was reachable in this book. Two of them are now, and the third waits on the digits.
